findings.paper_title: A&G Committee Report - Annual Internal Audit Report & Opinion 2025-26
findings.headline: Audit opinion is REASONABLE assurance, indicating identified weaknesses in governance or control framework
findings.detail: The Council's Chief Audit Executive concludes that REASONABLE assurance (rather than SUBSTANTIAL or FULL) can be given regarding governance, risk management and internal control. In audit terminology, REASONABLE assurance indicates the audit has identified gaps or weaknesses in the control framework, even though it remains generally adequate. The report also states 'There are no risks arising', suggesting identified weaknesses are manageable but present. Specific findings are detailed in the appended Annual Internal Audit Report.
findings.matters: Lenders assess financial risk partly through audit opinion on control and governance robustness; REASONABLE rather than SUBSTANTIAL assurance is audit language for 'we found problems', signalling control or governance gaps exist that require monitoring.
findings.figures: N/A
findings.quote: The Annual Internal Audit Report and Opinion appended to this report concludes that REASONABLE assurance can be given regarding the Council's framework of governance, risk management and internal control for the financial year 2025-26.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Internal Audit Tracker - Overdue Essential (ALL)
findings.headline: Government Procurement Card compliance gap: receipt retention procedures due 01/04/2026 remain unsigned and incomplete
findings.detail: An essential GPC audit recommendation on transaction receipt retention (six-year minimum per HMRC) is three months overdue. The updated User Guide awaits sign-off from the lead authority (CCC Finance Operations) and the Corporate Director before distribution. Status on other agreed actions is outstanding.
findings.matters: Unresolved HMRC compliance on receipt retention creates tax exposure and demonstrates governance process failures in procurement controls.
findings.figures: Due date 01/04/2026; minimum retention: 6 years
findings.quote: GPC User Guide updated and awaiting sign off from CCC (Finance Operations) before being sent to the Corporate Director – Finance & Procurement for sign off. Update on other elements of the agreed actions is awaited.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Internal Audit Tracker - Overdue Essential (ALL)
findings.headline: Property maintenance planning for commercial estate delayed 2–3 months due to resource constraints and software implementation problems
findings.detail: The planned maintenance programme for commercial properties, due 01/04/2026, is delayed. Condition surveys on ~70 HRA properties are underway, but the commercial property survey phase is held back by internal and external resource shortages. The Concerto software implementation encountered data import issues requiring the schedule to be halved.
findings.matters: Delayed proactive maintenance planning increases risk of unplanned emergency repairs and potential deferred maintenance liabilities on the asset base.
findings.figures: ~70 properties surveyed; 2–3 month delay forecast; element schedule initially too large, halved in size
findings.quote: delays are through lack of resource internal and external, the new property software system (Concerto) is still being modified as the imported element schedule was too large and unusable, this has been reviewed and halved in size.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Internal Audit Tracker - Overdue Essential (ALL)
findings.headline: General Ledger control and suspense account procedures nine months overdue, with sign-off and accountability gaps remaining
findings.detail: An essential audit recommendation due 31/10/2025 on GL control procedures remains incomplete. While management has substantially completed most actions, key gaps persist on revised control account sign-off, quality assurance arrangements, and monthly monitoring processes. Complex legacy account reconciliations are expected to take further time.
findings.matters: Unresolved GL control weaknesses undermine the reliability of the council's reported financial position and create governance gaps in core accounting controls.
findings.figures: Due date 31/10/2025; status as at 01/07/2026: 9 months overdue
findings.quote: Management has confirmed that majority of the remaining actions have now been substantially completed, with the exception of the implementation of revised control account sign-off, quality assurance and accountability arrangements. Remaining actions to close include resolving final gaps on the monthly monitoring process and legacy account reconciliation which are complex and will take longer to resolve.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Appendix A - Revenue Monitoring Report - 2025-26 Provisional Outturn
findings.headline: Interim Chief Finance Officer appointed June 2026 during period of significant structural financial strain
findings.detail: Council appointed Interim Chief Finance Officer (Martin Henry, from 1 June 2026) during a financial year marked by £7.0m overspend, £55.4m DSG deficit escalation, and complex contract management issues with Children's Trust. The permanent CFO role does not appear to be filled. The Chief Executive is also interim.
findings.matters: Finance leadership stability matters to lenders; an interim CFO during a period of structural budget challenge (particularly when paired with interim CEO) signals potential turnover or recruitment difficulty for senior finance roles in a complex environment.
findings.figures: Interim CFO appointed 01/06/2026; Interim CEO also in post; appointment made during provisional outturn period
findings.quote: (Interim) Chief Finance Officer Martin Henry 01/06/2026

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Appendix A - Revenue Monitoring Report - 2025-26 Provisional Outturn
findings.headline: Treasury management pressure reached £3.5m as capital investment and borrowing costs collide
findings.detail: Treasury management costs forecast £3.5m over budget, an increase of £0.6m since period 9, driven by capital investment requirements and interest rate forecasts. Concurrently, the £55.4m DSG deficit consumes cash reserves, tightening headroom for new borrowing and constraining financial flexibility.
findings.matters: Rising treasury costs reduce debt service capacity; a council holding a large DSG deficit with mounting borrowing pressures faces constrained financial flexibility and elevated credit risk to lenders.
findings.figures: £3.5m treasury pressure; £0.6m increase from period 9; DSG deficit £55.4m consuming cash
findings.quote: There is a forecast pressure within treasury management of £3.5m, an increase of £0.6m from period 9. The cost of treasury management is driven by capital investment requirements, interest rates forecasts, and availability of cash balances.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Appendix A - Revenue Monitoring Report - 2025-26 Provisional Outturn
findings.headline: Children's Trust overspent £17.4m with £0.6m of unresolved income uncertainty flagged to auditors
findings.detail: Northamptonshire Children's Trust (providing statutory children's social care for West and North Northamptonshire) overspent £17.4m (18% of budget). The position relies on NCT's Period 11 outturn, not yet finalised. Additionally, NCT has identified uncertainty on historic income from external organisations; a prudent provision of £0.6m has been made but remains under review with external auditors.
findings.matters: Children's social care is a statutory service—overspends cannot be cut; if NCT's final outturn worsens or the £0.6m income dispute resolves unfavourably, WNC absorbs the impact into general fund.
findings.figures: £17.4m overspend (18% of budget); £10.9m placement costs over budget; £2.4m non-deliverable savings; £0.6m income uncertainty provision; contracted sum £103.7m
findings.quote: The West Northamptonshire Council share of the countywide contract sum is £103.7m and the provisional outturn position is £121.0m which reflects an increase above the original contract sum of £17.4m.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Appendix A - Revenue Monitoring Report - 2025-26 Provisional Outturn
findings.headline: Adult social care nursing bed occupancy surged 23% with £12.1m overspend and efficiency headroom exhausted
findings.detail: Nursing placements following hospital discharge increased 23% by March 2026. Adult Social Care overspent £12.1m. The council's newly-formed Sustainability Programme (late 2025) acknowledges structural pressures. Prior savings initiatives (Positive Living Outcomes, Continuing Healthcare) are either exhausted or unachievable, indicating existing efficiency programmes have hit their ceiling.
findings.matters: Demand-driven overspends are recurring structural deficits; when efficiency options are exhausted, future budgets face sustained pressure—this signals persistent deficit risk unless service models fundamentally change.
findings.figures: 23% increase in nursing bed clients by March 2026; £12.1m overspend; £1.0m Continuing Healthcare savings unachieved; Positive Living Outcomes 'exhausted all further opportunities'
findings.quote: At the end of March 2026 there were 23% more clients in Nursing beds. The higher inflation costs are being driven in part by the 6.7% increase in the National Living Wage

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Appendix A - Revenue Monitoring Report - 2025-26 Provisional Outturn
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit jumped to £55.4m, driven by 88% EHCP growth since vesting
findings.detail: The DSG deficit grew from £21.5m to £55.4m in one year. The high needs block alone carries £64.5m deficit. The council reports 88% growth in Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) since vesting—larger than most councils nationally—forcing reliance on expensive independent placements due to lack of local state provision. Government support of £49.9m is expected but leaves the deficit partially uncovered.
findings.matters: Even with statutory override protection until 2028, this deficit drains general fund cash; when override lifts in 2028-29, council must absorb SEND costs from general fund, directly impacting debt service capacity.
findings.figures: Cumulative DSG deficit £55.4m (was £21.5m prior year); high needs block deficit £64.5m; EHCP growth 88%; expected HNSG support £49.9m
findings.quote: the overall accumulated deficit is £55.4m at the end of the current financial year, with the high needs block deficit making up £64.5m.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Appendix A - Revenue Monitoring Report - 2025-26 Provisional Outturn
findings.headline: £7.0m provisional overspend plus £4.0m of unachieved savings reveals £11m structural budget gap
findings.detail: The council spent £7.0m more than budget after deploying all £11.4m of general contingency reserves. Separately, £4.0m (16%) of the £24.6m planned savings did not materialise. Together, this £11m gap indicates the underlying budget was significantly optimistic about costs and savings delivery.
findings.matters: Councils with structural overspends and unachievable savings targets present higher credit risk; debt service becomes harder to sustain if this pattern repeats.
findings.figures: £7.0m overspend, £11.4m contingency deployed, £4.0m savings unachieved out of £24.6m planned (16% failure rate)
findings.quote: The forecast outturn position for 2025-26 is an overspend of £7.0m after the use of £11.4m of general budget contingencies, which were set aside in the budget for risks that may crystalise in the current financial year.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Appendix E - WNC Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Investment income fell short of benchmark and cash available for investment fell sharply due to DSG and borrowing pressures
findings.detail: Council's investment return was 4.08% vs 12-month SONIA benchmark of 4.55%, underperforming by 0.47 percentage points. This underperformance was not due to poor investment management but rather constrained cash balances: as DSG pressures and capital financing needs depleted reserves, less cash was available to invest even at favourable rates.
findings.matters: Shrinking cash balances reduce a council's buffer against future shocks and its ability to finance unexpected costs from reserves rather than borrowing.
findings.figures: Council return 4.08%, SONIA benchmark 4.55%, underperformance 0.47%, total investments outturn £142m vs plan £139m
findings.quote: During the year, the Council faced increased borrowing needs and ongoing cash pressures, including those arising from the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit. These pressures reduced the level of surplus cash available for investment for much of the year, limiting the Council's ability to benefit fully from higher short-term interest rates reflected in the SONIA benchmark.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Appendix E - WNC Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Financing cost burden increased to 2.7% of net revenue stream, up from 2.1% planned
findings.detail: The ratio of net financing costs (debt service) to net revenue stream deteriorated from budgeted 2.1% to actual 2.7%. This represents an additional strain on the revenue budget from debt obligations, driven by higher borrowing costs and the forced externalisation of borrowing mid-year.
findings.matters: Rising financing cost ratios directly reduce operational budget flexibility and indicate increasing structural debt service pressure. Lenders assess this metric closely as it shows what share of each revenue pound is committed to debt repayment.
findings.figures: Planned ratio 2.1%, outturn 2.7%
findings.quote: Ratio of financing costs to net revenue streams 2.1% 2.7%

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Appendix E - WNC Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit forced unplanned transition from internal to external borrowing mid-year
findings.detail: Cash balance reductions linked to DSG deficit pressures meant the council could not sustain its planned strategy of using internal cash to fund capital expenditure. It was forced to switch to external borrowing earlier and more extensively than the Treasury Management Strategy assumed. Section 5.3 states this placed pressure on the treasury budget.
findings.matters: DSG deficits signal unmanaged demand cost pressures (typically SEND/alternative provision) that the council cannot defer or control. When they force unplanned borrowing, they reveal structural budget stress that constrains financial flexibility.
findings.figures: CFR £987m, external borrowing £823m vs planned under-borrowing position of £331m, outturn only £164m under-borrowed
findings.quote: Ongoing cashflow pressures, particularly those linked to the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit, reduced the Council's available cash balances. This limited the Council's ability to continue using internal borrowing (funding capital expenditure from cash balances) and required a greater reliance on external borrowing earlier and to a greater extent than budgeted.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Appendix E - WNC Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Treasury outturn £3.5m adverse to budget, driven by forced external borrowing costs higher than planned
findings.detail: Council budgeted £8.6m net treasury costs but outturn was £12.1m. The variance stems from needing to externalise borrowing earlier and more extensively than planned, as cash balances depleted faster than expected. PWLB and Local Authority lending rates remained elevated despite Bank Rate falling to 3.75%, increasing the cost of forced borrowing.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted treasury cost increases indicate the council's cash planning broke down under unexpected pressure, forcing reactive and costly borrowing decisions rather than strategic ones.
findings.figures: Budget £8.6m, outturn £12.1m, adverse variance £3.5m, Bank Rate 3.75%, PWLB average rate 3.66%
findings.quote: The Treasury outturn shows an adverse variance of £3.5m, largely reflecting higher borrowing costs arising from the need to externalise internal borrowing during the year.

findings.paper_title: DSG Provisional Outturn including carry forward requests and school balances
findings.headline: Maintained school deficits increased to £786k from £443k (77% increase), with 7 of 8 schools in persistent deficit
findings.detail: Eight of 64 maintained schools were in deficit at 31 March 2026, with combined deficits totalling £786k, up from £443k in 2024-25. Seven of the eight schools were also in deficit in the prior year, indicating persistent financial difficulty. Deficits are primarily driven by falling rolls reducing budget allocations below fixed operating costs.
findings.matters: Persistent school-level deficits create vulnerability to service disruption and reputational risk; they require close oversight and may necessitate cross-subsidies from central reserves; worsening trajectory despite existing claw-back policies suggests schools cannot manage within allocated budgets.
findings.figures: £786k total school deficits (up from £443k); 8 of 64 schools in deficit; 7 of 8 schools persistent in deficit across 2024-25 and 2025-26
findings.quote: 8 of the 64 maintained schools were in deficit at the end of 2025-26 (8 in 2024-25) comprising a total deficit value of £786k in 2025-26 (£443k in 2024-25). The number of schools with deficits has remained the same as the prior year but the overall deficit value has increased by £343k. 7 of the schools in deficit at the end of 2024-25 were also those in deficit at the end of 2025-26.

findings.paper_title: DSG Provisional Outturn including carry forward requests and school balances
findings.headline: Government High Needs Stability Grant (£49.9m) is contingent on DfE accepting Local SEND Reform Plan, with payment delayed to autumn 2026
findings.detail: The government announced a HNSG to cover 90% of accumulated DSG deficits. WNC expects to receive £49.9m in autumn 2026, which would reduce the accumulated deficit from £55.4m to £5.5m. However, this payment is explicitly conditional on the Department for Education accepting the council's Local SEND Reform Plan. If the DfE does not accept the plan or delays acceptance, the council retains the full £55.4m deficit.
findings.matters: The deficit reduction pathway depends on government grant contingent on plan acceptance, creating execution risk; if the grant is not received as expected, the council's deficit position remains as reported; payment timing in autumn 2026 means acceptance decision is imminent.
findings.figures: £49.9m HNSG expected; £55.4m current accumulated deficit; grant covers 90% of accumulated deficit to end 2025-26
findings.quote: This grant will cover 90% of DSG deficits accrued by local authorities up to the end of the 2025-26 financial year, to be paid in the Autumn of 2026 following DfE accepting the LA's Local SEND Reform Plan

findings.paper_title: DSG Provisional Outturn including carry forward requests and school balances
findings.headline: Council has set an intentional £65.4m deficit budget for high needs block in 2026-27, indicating structural deficit will continue and worsen
findings.detail: Rather than attempt to eliminate or reduce the high needs deficit in 2026-27, the council has explicitly set a £65.4m deficit budget, defined as the gap between government funding allocation and estimated demand and growth. This planned deficit is larger than the 2025-26 overspend of £36.3m, showing the council expects the structural gap to widen year-on-year.
findings.matters: Planned year-on-year deficits demonstrate no path to structural balance; the council is funding operations from reserves rather than suppressing demand or improving efficiency; continued accumulation of deficits will exhaust reserves and create dependency on government support.
findings.figures: £65.4m deficit budget set for 2026-27 high needs block (vs £36.3m overspend in 2025-26)
findings.quote: The Council has set a deficit budget on the High Needs Block for 2026-27 totalling £65.4m which is the gap between the high needs funding allocation from government, and the estimated demand and growth over the next year

findings.paper_title: DSG Provisional Outturn including carry forward requests and school balances
findings.headline: 88% increase in Education Health and Care Plans since vesting is larger than most councils nationally, driving high needs overspend of £36.3m
findings.detail: WNC has experienced an 88% increase in EHCPs since vesting, significantly above the national pattern. This exceptional growth in demand for special educational needs provision is coupled with inadequate local supply, forcing the council to resort to expensive independent sector placements. The high needs block overspent by £36.3m, with independent sector and out-of-area costs alone exceeding budget by £14.3m.
findings.matters: Demand growth substantially above plan indicates a structural mismatch between available funding and service requirements; forced reliance on expensive independent providers is higher-cost solution than planned provision; this scale of growth is unlikely to reverse and will persist as a budget pressure.
findings.figures: 88% increase in EHCPs since vesting; £36.3m high needs block overspend; £14.3m independent sector overspend
findings.quote: WNC has seen an 88% increase in Education Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) since vesting day which is larger than most other councils nationally

findings.paper_title: DSG Provisional Outturn including carry forward requests and school balances
findings.headline: Accumulated DSG deficit of £55.4m explicitly reducing council's cash balances and contributing to treasury management pressures
findings.detail: The DSG deficit has grown from £21.5m carried forward to £55.4m, a £33.9m deterioration in-year. The paper explicitly states these deficits 'reduce the Council's cash balances, limiting funds available for investment and directly contributing to the Treasury Management pressures being faced.' This represents a material impact on the council's liquidity position and financial headroom.
findings.matters: Lenders assess liquidity and cash availability as a key indicator of financial stability; DSG deficits converting to cash outflow and explicitly impacting treasury management signals constrained borrowing capacity and reduced financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £55.4m accumulated DSG deficit (up from £21.5m); £33.9m in-year overspend
findings.quote: these deficits reduce the Council's cash balances, limiting funds available for investment and directly contributing to the Treasury Management pressures being faced

findings.detail: Disabled adaptations within the HRA spent £3.111m against a budget of £2.3m. The council attributes the £811k overspend to sustained demand for adaptations to enable tenants to remain safely and independently in their own homes, reflecting ongoing cost pressures in this area.

The scale of this increase has prompted the council to acknowledge forecasting weaknesses and commit to improved programme monitoring and early risk identification.
findings.matters: Significant unexplained slippage indicates capital forecasting accuracy issues and potential delivery risks that affect council financial stability and debt financing timelines

findings.paper_title: Strategic Risk Register - Appendix A - SR14 - Financial Sustainability (1)
findings.headline: Financial Sustainability risk live since 2021 and rated as Likely to occur with Catastrophic impact
findings.detail: SR14 has been on the risk register since April 2021. The risk is driven by increasing demand for services, rising service costs, and uncertainty in local government funding. The Audit and Governance Committee reviewed it as recently as 25 February 2026.
findings.matters: A five-year-old, live catastrophic risk suggests structural challenges to the council's funding model that have not been resolved. Lenders assess whether such risks are temporary or endemic to the authority's finances.
findings.figures: Risk added 01/04/2021; last reviewed 25/02/2026; Impact 5 - Catastrophic; Likelihood 4 - Likely
findings.quote: Increasing demand for services, increasing cost of services and uncertainty relating to local government funding is a continuing risk to the Council which needs to be closely and carefully monitored

findings.paper_title: Strategic Risk Register - Appendix A - SR14 - Financial Sustainability (1)
findings.headline: Financial position for 25/26 has worsened with little time to correct in-year
findings.detail: The council explicitly states the financial position for 2025/26 has deteriorated since the previous report, and there is insufficient time remaining in the financial year to bring it back into balance. This worsening prompted an upward revision of the risk assessment.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council's budget is tracking to balance and whether management has a credible plan to recover mid-year. A deteriorating position with no in-year fix signals potential pressure on reserves or need for emergency action.

findings.paper_title: Appendix K - West Northamptonshire Council TMSS 2026-27
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement and total debt rising substantially across the medium term
findings.detail: The council's CFR (underlying borrowing need) rises from £1,350m in 2026/27 to £1,441m by 2029/30. Total debt (including PFI and finance leases) rises from £1,175m to £1,445m over the same period. This rising trajectory is driven by the capital programme and the forced externalization of internal borrowing due to DSG deficit pressures.
findings.matters: Rising debt increases future refinancing risks and interest cost pressures, particularly material given the uncertain interest rate environment and the council's diminishing ability to manage debt through internal resources.
findings.quote: The rising trend of the Authorised Limit reflects that of the CFR net of internal borrowing and subsequently the Operational Boundary.

findings.paper_title: Appendix K - West Northamptonshire Council TMSS 2026-27
findings.headline: The accumulated DSG deficit is forcing earlier externalization of borrowing at current PWLB rates
findings.detail: The council maintains an internal under-borrowed position (using cash balances rather than external loans), but the accumulated Dedicated Schools Grant deficit reduces available liquidity and forces the externalisation of borrowing earlier than planned. This year's external borrowing budget is £322m, of which £195m is treasury management borrowing (externalizing internal borrowing and refinancing maturing debt) rather than capital expenditure. The council would prefer to defer longer-term borrowing, awaiting forecast rate falls, but the DSG deficit prevents this.
findings.matters: Earlier externalization at current PWLB rates (5yr at 4.81%, 10yr at 5.39%) instead of waiting for forecast falls increases long-term debt costs. For lenders, this affects cash flow resilience and refinancing risk; for the finance director, it signals a structural liquidity constraint.
findings.figures: External borrowing 2026/27: £322m total (£127m capital, £195m treasury management). Current 5yr PWLB 4.81%, 10yr 5.39%. Forecast 5yr PWLB to fall to 4.1% by Q4 2027.
findings.quote: the scope to continue internal borrowing is increasingly constrained by the accumulated Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit. While the DSG deficit does not form part of the CFR and does not increase the Council's underlying capital borrowing requirement, it represents a cash-backed pressure on liquidity and reduces the level of internal resources available to support borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Final Budget and Medium Term Plan Report 2026-27 - Full Council v3

findings.detail: The approved capital programme includes £47.1m in prudential borrowing over five years (£17.6m in 2026-27). This will add £20.9m in revenue implications (interest and MRP) over the medium term. The council's policy is to 'minimise the need for borrowing' but the current capital programme requires substantial debt financing.
findings.matters: Each pound borrowed increases the council's debt servicing burden. With social care demand pressures consuming contingency and the medium-term plan already showing a £42.5m gap, significant new borrowing adds to the revenue pressure in future years.
findings.figures: £47.1m prudential borrowing 2026-31; £17.6m in 2026-27; £20.9m revenue implications (interest and MRP)

findings.paper_title: Final Budget and Medium Term Plan Report 2026-27 - Full Council v3
findings.headline: Treasury function under strain from DSG deficit affecting working capital management
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that the growing DSG deficit 'increases the demand on the Council's working capital, placing additional strain on treasury resources and contributing to the overall pressure on cash management.' Treasury growth of £4.2m has been budgeted to support this, driven by increased borrowing requirements and a challenging interest rate environment despite recent modest reductions.
findings.matters: A constrained treasury position reduces the council's ability to manage in-year cash movements and restricts borrowing capacity for investments or emergencies. This is a warning sign about overall financial resilience.
findings.figures: £4.2m treasury growth in 2026-27 budget; DSG deficit draining working capital
findings.quote: These pressures are materially impacted by the growing Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit. Although DSG is ring-fenced, the deficit increases the demand on the Council's working capital, placing additional strain on treasury resources and contributing to the overall pressure on cash management.

findings.paper_title: Final Budget and Medium Term Plan Report 2026-27 - Full Council v3
findings.headline: Adult social care demand growing faster than anticipated: nursing care placements up >20% since April 2025
findings.detail: Adult Social Care budgeted growth of £9.0m is driven by both volume and complexity. The council reports that from 1 April 2025, the number of clients with services has grown 6% overall, with nursing care placements up more than 20%. The document attributes this to hospital discharge processes and people accessing care later in life with more severe health conditions. This growth is expected to continue.
findings.matters: A 20% surge in the highest-cost care setting (nursing) is a significant pressure that may not be fully captured in budget assumptions. If this trend continues, the £9.0m growth allocation may prove insufficient.
findings.figures: 6% growth in client numbers overall; >20% growth in nursing care placements; £9.0m budgeted growth
findings.quote: The number of individuals entering nursing care provision has risen by more than 20% since the beginning of the year. This surge is partly driven by hospital discharge processes and highlights a growing pattern where people are accessing Adult Social Care later in life and often with more severe health conditions.

findings.paper_title: Final Budget and Medium Term Plan Report 2026-27 - Full Council v3
findings.headline: Council already at maximum council tax rate with limited flexibility; 4.95% increase includes 2% adult social care precept
findings.detail: The 2026-27 budget includes a 4.95% council tax rise (2.95% core + 2% adult social care precept), described as being 'in line with referendum threshold limits.' This generates £16.6m of new revenue. With both core and social care precept at or near maximum allowable levels, the council has minimal room to increase council tax further without crossing the referendum threshold and triggering a local vote.
findings.matters: Council tax is increasingly the council's only flexible revenue source. Exhausting this flexibility limits future options for addressing the £42.5m MTFP gap without either service cuts or reserves drawdown.
findings.figures: 4.95% increase (2.95% + 2% precept); £16.6m additional revenue; assumes 1.1% taxbase growth
findings.quote: This has been set in line with referendum threshold limits and legislative guidance confirmed within the Local Authority Final Settlement.

findings.paper_title: Final Budget and Medium Term Plan Report 2026-27 - Full Council v3
findings.headline: Medium-term plan forecasts £42.5m cumulative deficit over four years, starting at £24.2m in 2027-28 (5% of budget)
findings.detail: The MTFP shows an incremental budget gap of £24.2m for 2027-28 (5% of net budget), declining to 1% by 2030-31, with a cumulative gap of £42.5m over the period. The council states 'these estimates are based on the best information we have at this point in time' but acknowledges 'the MTFP position does not look as daunting as in previous years it often sees significant shifts upwards when the budget refresh takes place.' The projections assume delivery of £29m in annual efficiencies.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess the realism of the MTFP. The council explicitly warns that the gap typically worsens during the year. The forecast depends entirely on delivering £29m in annual savings; any shortfall in demand management or efficiency delivery creates an unplanned deficit.
findings.figures: £24.2m gap 2027-28 (5% of budget); £42.5m cumulative gap 2027-31; assumes £29m annual savings delivery
findings.quote: Whilst the MTFP position does not look as daunting as in previous years it often sees significant shifts upwards when the budget refresh takes place as a result of what we actually begin to see on the service pressures as we get into the new financial year.

findings.paper_title: Final Budget and Medium Term Plan Report 2026-27 - Full Council v3
findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision requirement jumps £7.6m annually as one-off funding provision fully depleted
findings.detail: MRP (the amount set aside annually to repay debt principal) was previously funded through a one-time provision that has now been exhausted. The council must now budget £7.6m annually from 2026-27 onwards to cover repayment of prior years' capital spending and estimated 2025-26 completions. This is a new, recurring cost with no offsetting savings identified.
findings.matters: This is a structural increase in the council's debt servicing cost with no corresponding revenue saving. It reduces the council's ability to absorb other pressures.
findings.figures: £7.6m annual MRP growth requirement from 2026-27 onwards
findings.quote: Previously, this was funded through a provision which is one off funding. That provision has now been fully utilised and therefore, the budget for 2026-27 includes required growth of £7.6m to cover payments relating to prior years and the estimate of completions expected in the current 2025-26 financial year.

findings.paper_title: Final Budget and Medium Term Plan Report 2026-27 - Full Council v3
findings.headline: General contingency fully utilized in current and prior years; council now relying on replenished reserve to absorb recurring pressures
findings.detail: The 2025-26 contingency of £11.4m has been fully committed to offset demand-led overspends. The council has prudently increased the 2026-27 contingency from draft budget by £3.1m (to £10.1m) using the improved settlement position. However, the pattern—full utilization in both current and prior years—indicates the council is consistently forecasting below actual demand, particularly in social care services.
findings.matters: Repeated full utilization of contingency signals that the base budget assumptions for demand-led services are understated. A lender should question whether the £10.1m contingency for 2026-27 is sufficient given historical pattern.
findings.figures: £11.4m contingency fully utilized in 2025-26; contingency fully used in prior years; £10.1m set aside for 2026-27 (up £3.1m from draft)
findings.quote: The general contingency budget set aside to manage risk within the budget has proved vital over the past few years, with the 2025-26 balance currently fully utilised in year. Therefore, the prudent decision has been taken to transfer the remaining balance of additional funding to general contingency to strengthen the contingency budget going forward resulting in an overall balance of £10.1m.

findings.paper_title: Final Budget and Medium Term Plan Report 2026-27 - Full Council v3
findings.headline: Children's Trust contract contains £17.7m structural deficit with £14.9m driven by placement demand alone
findings.detail: The joint Northamptonshire Children's Trust contract sum agreed at £200.8m (£195.2m core) includes a £17.7m structural deficit at county level, driven substantially by £14.9m in rising care placement costs. The council notes this 'is indicative of the national picture of rising costs of children's social care.' The split between West and North Northamptonshire councils for 2026-27 remains unresolved (paragraph 6.21), suggesting negotiation over burden-sharing.
findings.matters: This is not a one-off pressure but a structural deficit in a fundamental statutory service. The council cannot avoid this cost. If WNC bears the larger share, it will require either additional reserves or further budget reductions elsewhere.
findings.figures: £200.8m contract; £17.7m structural deficit at county level; £14.9m placement cost growth
findings.quote: A total contract sum totalling £200.8m has been agreed for 2026-27... The increase in the core contract sum is formed of £17.7m structural deficit position informed by the forecast outturn for this financial year and how these pressures on placement demand are expected to materialise in the next financial year.

findings.paper_title: Final Budget and Medium Term Plan Report 2026-27 - Full Council v3
findings.headline: High Needs Block in cumulative structural deficit of £65.3m with insufficient funding to address demand
findings.detail: The DSG High Needs Block is forecast to overspend by £37.1m in 2025-26 alone, sitting within a cumulative deficit of £65.3m. The 2026-27 allocation increases funding by only £0.5m (0.5%), far below inflation and demand growth. The council is in the bottom quartile nationally for high needs funding per pupil. The government's statutory override protecting councils from consolidating these deficits into the general fund runs only until March 2028, after which only 90% of historical deficits will be covered via a High Needs Stability Grant.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether this £65m+ liability will transfer to the general fund after 2028, creating a cliff-edge funding problem. Even with the government's promised takeover from 2028-29, the council faces material unfunded risk through 2027-28.
findings.figures: £37.1m overspend 2025-26; £65.3m cumulative deficit; £85.5m allocation (0.5% increase); bottom quartile per-pupil funding nationally
findings.quote: with the current year level of overspend within the WNC High Needs Block forecast at £37.1m (£65.3m cumulative), the funding is insufficient and therefore the Council is looking at cumulative, structural deficits continuing as demand and inflation outstrips funding increases.

findings.paper_title: Appendix G(i) WNC Capital Strategy 26-27 Final
findings.headline: Nearly half of General Fund capital programme (46.7%) is funded from external sources over which council has limited influence
findings.detail: Grant funding accounts for 16.19% (£19.7m) and external contributions 30.47% (£37.0m) of the £121.5m General Fund capital programme. Council explicitly acknowledges it has 'limited influence' over these sources, which are shaped by central government policy and developer activity. This creates structural budget uncertainty.
findings.matters: External funding sources are uncontrollable; if grant allocations are reduced or development activity slows, council must either reduce capital investment, increase borrowing, or draw on reserves
findings.figures: Grant Funding: £19,671k (16.19% of total); External Funding: £37,026k (30.47%); combined external: £56,697k out of £121,513k total
findings.quote: The Council only has limited influence over the external and grant funding sources and the Council's Capital Programme will continue to be largely influenced by central government policy.

findings.paper_title: Appendix G(i) WNC Capital Strategy 26-27 Final
findings.headline: Council's future capital receipts severely limited because Strategic Land Holdings are only sizeable asset ownership, with receipt timing unpredictable
findings.detail: The paper explicitly states that receipts are only 'potential' because Strategic Land Holdings (SLH) are the only area of significant asset ownership under the council's control. The council acknowledges that predicting timescales and values is problematic due to the complex nature of these sites and multiple interests of partners, developers and local groups.
findings.matters: Severely constrains the council's ability to self-fund capital investment or quickly repay borrowing through asset disposals; increases structural reliance on borrowing and external funding sources
findings.figures: Limited to Strategic Land Holdings only; no other material property assets available for disposal
findings.quote: Receipts are referred to as potential because Strategic Land Holdings (SLH) remain the only area of sizeable asset ownership under the Council's control. However, predicting the timescales and values of receipts on these areas is problematic due to the complex nature of these sites and the multiple interests of partners, developers and local interest groups.

findings.paper_title: Appendix G(i) WNC Capital Strategy 26-27 Final
findings.headline: Forward funding strategy creates cash flow risk by betting on future S106 and CIL receipts to repay borrowed funds
findings.detail: The North West Relief Road (major transport scheme) is being forward funded with discretionary borrowing, with repayment planned from future S106 and CIL developer contributions that will be received several years after project completion. The policy states forward funding is exceptional, but this scheme demonstrates it is being used for major infrastructure.
findings.matters: If developer contributions are delayed, suspended, or fail to materialize as expected, council faces cash flow pressure and higher debt servicing costs on borrowed funds awaiting repayment from these income sources
findings.figures: Forward funding applied to major scheme with S106 and CIL receipts received 'several years after the completion of the project'
findings.quote: Those schemes will be forward funded with Discretionary funding, which will be repaid when the relevant CIL and s.106 are received. The main scheme to which this applies is the Northampton North West Relief Road.

findings.paper_title: Appendix G(i) WNC Capital Strategy 26-27 Final
findings.headline: Council took in-house the HRA development part of the capital programme from Northamptonshire Partnership Homes in 2025
findings.detail: Previously managed by a partner, the new development element of the HRA capital programme is now being managed directly by the council's management team and Housing Improvement Board. This represents a significant operational shift bringing £364.4m of HRA capital investment under direct council management and responsibility.
findings.matters: Transfer of operational control and management risk from an external partner to the council; HRA capital programme is substantial and success of in-house delivery directly affects financial position
findings.figures: HRA Capital Programme total £364,350k over five years (2026-31)
findings.quote: The Council took back in house the HRA new development part of the Capital Programme from Northamptonshire Partnership Homes in 2025.

findings.paper_title: Council Report Final HRA Budget 2026-27 and MTFP CLEAN
findings.headline: New build program rebalanced downward (£10.4m reduction) with deliverable units uncertain; reallocation to acquisitions strategy may indicate delivery challenges.
findings.detail: Between draft and final budget, the New Build Programme was reduced by £10.4m and rebalanced to Acquisitions (+£14.3m). The council reallocated £8m from New Build to Acquisitions/Buybacks and incorporated a further £4m LAHF R4 programme. A £1.6m rephasing adjustment for Avenue Campus suggests ongoing construction delays. The council notes it 'currently programmed to deliver approximately 150 dwellings per year across the MTFP' but the medium-term outlook shows declining units: 150 units p.a. years 1-5, then 125 p.a. years 6-10, then 100 p.a. years 11-30, then replacement RTB sales only year 31+.
findings.matters: New build provides future rental income growth and replaces stock lost to Right to Buy. A shift from new build to acquisitions (purchasing existing stock) is lower-risk but also delivers lower net stock growth and may indicate delivery challenges on new schemes. The rephasing of Avenue Campus and the declining delivery trajectory (150→125→100 units p.a.) suggest the council is moderating ambitions due to finance, planning, or project delivery constraints. This affects the HRA's long-term income sustainability.
findings.figures: New Build reduction £10.4m; Acquisitions increase £14.3m; Avenue Campus rephasing £1.6m; planned delivery: 150 units p.a. years 1-5, declining to 40 RTB replacement by year 31
findings.quote: The principal changes to the 2026/27 capital programme since publication of the draft budget reflect a £10.4m rebalancing between the New Build Programme and the Acquisitions programme. The new build programme is continuously monitored and reviewed along with the Council's HRA prudential borrowing and affordability.

findings.paper_title: Council Report Final HRA Budget 2026-27 and MTFP CLEAN
findings.headline: Decent Homes Standard revision from 2035 onwards will impose new costs to social housing that have not yet been quantified or budgeted.
findings.detail: Current assessment shows 19.15% of stock (2,201 homes) non-decent as at year-end 2024-25. The council has budgeted £2.2m in 2026-27 to achieve 8% non-decency by year-end. However, government has announced a revised Decent Homes Standard to apply from 2035-37. The report states: 'Guidance is to be published in due course. The results of this guidance will be built into future Medium Term Financial plans, once quantified.' No cost estimate exists yet.
findings.matters: A revised Decent Homes Standard likely to impose more stringent energy efficiency, thermal, or safety requirements. The lack of early cost quantification means the council has not budgeted for what could be a large capital commitment. If the standard is significantly more demanding than current delivery (e.g., EPC ratings, insulation, heating systems), the cost to bring all stock into compliance by 2037 could be material and may require additional borrowing or subsidy.
findings.figures: 19.15% non-decent (2,201 homes) at end 2024-25; £2.2m budgeted 2026-27 to reduce to 8%; EPC C standard: £3.7m in MTFP to 2030, additional costs thereafter not yet quantified
findings.quote: There will be a detailed design of a modernised Decent Homes Standard that will apply to social and private rented homes from 2035. Guidance is to be published in due course. The results of this guidance will be built into future Medium Term Financial plans, once quantified.

findings.paper_title: Council Report Final HRA Budget 2026-27 and MTFP CLEAN
findings.headline: Welfare reform risk: if Local Housing Allowance rates remain frozen, rent collection will come under pressure as the gap between tenants' benefits and rising rents widens.
findings.detail: LHA rates were frozen from 1 April 2025. The council notes that the Autumn Statement and subsequent announcements contained no decision to unfreeze LHA rates; the council explicitly states 'We await further information between draft and final budgets.' The report warns: 'If welfare LHA allowances potentially frozen again the gap between Rents and benefits will grow, putting more pressure on vulnerable tenants to maintain their rentals.' The council is proceeding on the assumption that welfare will match CPI (3.8%), but this is uncertain and at risk.
findings.matters: LHA rates determine what government-supported tenants can claim for rent. If frozen while rents rise 4.8%, vulnerable tenants face a real-terms loss of £4-8 per week. This drives rent arrears and bad debt. The council's P9 2025-26 position notes 'forecast rent arrears are rising at a much lower rate than previously anticipated' — but this assumed welfare support would keep pace with costs. A continued freeze would reverse this improvement.
findings.figures: LHA frozen since 1 April 2025; rent increase 4.8% (average weekly rent rising £5.51 to £120.31); welfare support assumed to rise 3.8% (CPI)
findings.quote: With welfare LHA allowances potentially frozen again the gap between Rents and benefits will grow, putting more pressure on vulnerable tenants to maintain their rentals. A decision to unfreeze LHA rates was absent in the Statements. We await further information between draft and final budgets.

findings.paper_title: Council Report Final HRA Budget 2026-27 and MTFP CLEAN
findings.headline: Working balance projected at only £1m above the statutory £5m minimum, with the Service Improvement Reserve depleted to zero.
findings.detail: HRA working balances are projected to be £6m at the start of 2026-27 and remain at £6m year-end, against an assessed minimum of £5m. This leaves a buffer of only £1m above the minimum safety level. Additionally, the HRA Service Improvement Reserve is drawn down from £209k to £0 by year-end 2026-27 (Table 4). The General Reserve is projected to reduce from £6,155k to £7,032k by the end of the year. The council notes it is 'prudently' transferring £2.5m into reserves during 2026-27, but this action itself indicates concern about future resilience.
findings.matters: Reserves at minimum level indicate limited financial resilience. If the council faces unexpected costs (compliance failures, urgent repairs, bad debt spikes) or income shortfalls (welfare reform impacts on rent collection, void increases), it has minimal buffer before needing to cut services or breach statutory minimums. The transfer of £2.5m into reserves suggests the council recognizes this tightness.
findings.figures: Working balance £6m (£1m above £5m minimum); Service Improvement Reserve £0 (from £209k); General Reserve £7,032k year-end; reserves transfer in year £2,471k
findings.quote: Based on the latest reserve position, working balances are projected to be around £1m above this minimum level. A further £2.5m has been transferred to reserves as a prudent measure to strengthen the HRA's financial resilience and mitigate future risks

findings.paper_title: Council Report Final HRA Budget 2026-27 and MTFP CLEAN
findings.headline: Interest Cover Ratio of 1.37 is tight to the minimum 1.25 target and explicitly depends on budget assumptions holding.
findings.detail: The Interest Cover Ratio (ICR) measures whether the net cost of services covers the cost of borrowing. For 2026-27, the council forecasts an ICR of 1.37 against a sector target minimum of 1.25. However, the council explicitly warns that 'sustaining the ICR above the recommended level depends on the revenue budget operating within the assumptions set out in this report, particularly achieving the income levels, expenditure controls and savings included within the revenue proposals.' Any shortfall in rent income, slippage in efficiencies, or spending overspend could push the ICR below 1.25.
findings.matters: The ICR is the key metric lenders use to assess housing authority debt serviceability. An ICR this close to minimum with acknowledged dependency on assumptions means the authority has limited headroom. Any adverse variance in income (e.g., rent arrears, void losses) or expenditure (e.g., compliance costs) could breach safe levels and trigger need for urgent financial restructuring.
findings.figures: ICR 2026-27: 1.37; minimum target 1.25; sector threshold for concern typically 1.25-1.3
findings.quote: For 2026-27, the ICR is forecast at 1.37, compared with the minimum target of 1.25. However, sustaining the ICR above the recommended level depends on the revenue budget operating within the assumptions set out in this report, particularly achieving the income levels, expenditure controls and savings included within the revenue proposals.

findings.paper_title: Council Report Final HRA Budget 2026-27 and MTFP CLEAN
findings.headline: HRA Capital Financing Requirement rises to £519.5m by 2030-31 with debt peaking at £720.2m; new borrowing of £37.5m in 2026-27 alone.
findings.detail: The council is undertaking significant borrowing to fund new housing delivery, acquisitions, and stock improvements. The HRACFR (amount the HRA must borrow) rises every year from £308.1m at April 2026 to £519.5m by March 2031. Cumulative new borrowing across the MTFP totals approximately £206m (years 2026-31). Over the 40-year business plan, debt is projected to peak at £720.2m in year 29 before declining. The 2026-27 capital program totals £82.5m.
findings.matters: The scale and trajectory of HRA borrowing is substantial. For a lender, the rising debt profile and the fact that the council will carry peak borrowing of £720m for years 11-29 of the plan affects credit risk assessment. The council's ability to service this debt depends entirely on the income and cost assumptions in this budget holding true.
findings.figures: HRACFR: £308.1m (2026-27) rising to £519.5m (2030-31); new borrowing 2026-27 £37.5m; debt peak £720.2m in year 29; capital expenditure 2026-27 £82.5m
findings.quote: Table 6 shows that the level of the HRACFR is rising in every year of the MTFP. The HRA business plan model shows this level of borrowing is sustainable over the medium term and also over the life of the 40 year business plan

findings.paper_title: Council Report Final HRA Budget 2026-27 and MTFP CLEAN
findings.headline: Council housing regulator graded the authority C3 and now requires monthly reporting on compliance failures.
findings.detail: Following a self-referral by the council, the Regulator of Social Housing issued a C3 grading in November 2024. The council has been reporting monthly to the regulator since January 2025 on progress against a Business Improvement Action Plan. The original self-referral was triggered by 'due diligence undertaken under WNC's new responsibilities as the Responsible Body for Council housing stock condition' which 'has identified issues relating to safety standards and compliance that could put the Council in breach of regulations and tenants at risk.'
findings.matters: A C3 regulator rating indicates material governance and compliance failures in housing management. Monthly regulatory reporting suggests ongoing concerns about the council's ability to manage social housing safely and in compliance with regulations. This affects lender confidence and the council's operational capacity.
findings.figures: C3 grading (November 2024); monthly reporting since January 2025
findings.quote: Following the Council's regulatory self-referral and subsequent C3 grading in November 2024, Cabinet approved a Business Improvement Action plan detailing the key areas of improvement required in order to return to regulatory compliance. Since January 2025, the Council has been reporting to the Regulator on a monthly basis, providing regular updates on property health and safety compliance

findings.paper_title: Appendix K - West Northamptonshire Council TMSS 2026-27
findings.headline: Accumulated DSG deficit is constraining internal borrowing and forcing earlier externalisation of debt
findings.detail: The council's accumulated Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit is reducing available cash resources and limiting the ability to finance capital spending through internal borrowing (using reserves and cash balances). To manage this liquidity constraint, the council is forced to externalise internal borrowing earlier than otherwise planned, increasing external debt from PWLB and other lenders. The document explicitly states this has resulted in increased treasury management borrowing, primarily to convert what would previously have been internal borrowing into external debt.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that the council's treasury flexibility is constrained by the DSG deficit consuming available liquidity. This directly affects the council's cash management position and increases reliance on external borrowing, reducing financial flexibility and refinancing options.
findings.figures: External borrowing planned for capital: £127m (2026/27) declining to £58m (2027/28); Treasury management borrowing: £195m (2026/27), declining to £164m (2027/28); Current net borrowing position: £647.1m
findings.quote: As liquidity constraints arising from the DSG deficit limit the ability to sustain internal borrowing, a greater proportion of borrowing is required to be externalised earlier than would otherwise have been the case. This has resulted in an increase in treasury management borrowing, primarily reflecting the externalisation of internal borrowing and the refinancing of maturing debt

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Grant Thornton's Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Prior-year recommendation to reconcile custodian holdings quarterly has been implemented; prior incident of missing investment (£462k) was isolated but highlighted data completeness risk
findings.detail: In the prior year audit, an investment asset was not included in the custodian's holdings report and was excluded from financial statements. This has now been resolved through new quarterly reconciliation processes between Northern Trust (custodian), CBRE (investment manager), and the Fund's Nuveen asset. Weekly meetings with Northern Trust in the run-up to year-end close now ensure all statements are captured. Auditor confirmed no completeness issues were identified in 2024/25 testing.
findings.matters: This shows the Fund had a material data completeness control gap that could have resulted in unrecorded assets. Whilst now remediated, it indicates the Fund's asset management information systems have had accuracy issues that took time to fix.
findings.figures: Missing asset in prior year: £462k (trivial but represents a completeness risk); no issues identified in 2024/25 follow-up testing
findings.quote: an investment asset that was not included in the Custodian's holdings report and was therefore excluded from the draft financial statements. This investment has been valued by the fund manager at £462k at 31 March 2024… Further processes and controls have been put in place to check the custodians' holdings quarterly.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Grant Thornton's Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Net assets increased from £3,618.9m to £3,748.2m year-on-year, but next triennial valuation (2025) expected Q1 2026 will be critical
findings.detail: The Fund's net assets increased by £129.3m in the year to 31 March 2025. The 2022 triennial valuation showed the Fund had assets sufficient to cover 113% of accrued liabilities (a surplus position). However, the 2025 triennial valuation is now well progressed and expected to be published in Q1 2026. Given potential market movements since 2022, this valuation will be a key test of the Fund's funding adequacy.
findings.matters: A finance director and lender need to know the Fund's true funding position and trajectory. Triennial valuations determine employer contribution rates and reveal any unfunded liabilities that could force the council to increase pension contributions, reducing resources available for council services.
findings.figures: Net assets 31 Mar 2025: £3,748.2m (prior year: £3,618.9m), increase of £129.3m; 2022 triennial: 113% funding level
findings.quote: The net assets of the Northamptonshire Pension Fund as at the end of March 2025 amounted to £3,748.2m (31 March 2024: £3,618.9m). The 2022 triennial valuation was undertaken by Hymans Robertson, and showed that the Fund had assets sufficient to cover 113% of the accrued liabilities as at 31 March 2022. The 2025 triennial valuation is now well progressed and expected to be published in the first quarter of 2026.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Grant Thornton's Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Fund moving from ACCESS asset pool to Border to Coast Pension Partnership (BCPP) following Government rejection of ACCESS's FCA-regulation proposal
findings.detail: Following the Government's May 2025 response to the Fit for the Future consultation, the Fund concluded that BCPP is its preferred pooling partner and has submitted an expression of interest alongside six other LGPS funds from ACCESS. Further due diligence and governance steps are underway to progress the transition, including obtaining approval from BCPP partner funds.
findings.matters: Asset pooling transitions involve operational and governance risks. A move from one pool to another signals regulatory pressure on the current arrangement and introduces execution risk during transition that could temporarily affect investment performance or fund costs.
findings.figures: Seven LGPS funds (including Northamptonshire) have submitted expressions of interest to join BCPP; 160 active employers covered by the Fund
findings.quote: Following an evaluation process to determine alternative pooling options, the Fund concluded that Border to Coast Pension Partnership (BCPP) is its preferred pooling partner. An expression of interest to join BCPP has been submitted, alongside six other LGPS funds from ACCESS.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Grant Thornton's Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Management fees expense recognition error identified in BlueBay Investments where costs for wrong financial period were charged
findings.detail: CTI reports from investment manager Waystone covered January 2024–December 2024 but were fully charged to the 2024/25 financial year instead of being pro-rated for April–December 2024, and the final quarter (January–March 2025) was not charged at all. Auditor flagged this as a potential control deficiency. Management stated it was an isolated incident due to delayed receipt of a key report and that other controls (annual report cost transparency and reconciliation) should have caught it.
findings.matters: Expense misstatement and timing issues affect fund returns and performance reporting. While this instance was immaterial, it reveals weaknesses in the Fund's controls over expense recognition that could allow material misstatement of investment costs.
findings.figures: Period covered: 31 Jan 2024–31 Dec 2024; financial year scope: 1 Apr 2024–31 Mar 2025; error detected in audit sampling
findings.quote: the reporting period for these costs was from 31 January 2024 to 31 December 2024. However, the entire amount was charged in the current financial year, rather than applying a pro-rata allocation for the period 1 April 2024 to 31 December 2024, which aligns with the financial year

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Grant Thornton's Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: £308m of investments misclassified between fair value hierarchy levels, requiring reclassification across L1, L2 and L3
findings.detail: During testing, auditors identified that one pooled property investment (£13.6m) and one pooled investment (£285.3m) were mistakenly classified as Level 1 when they should be Level 2, and another property investment (£9.2m) was classified as Level 3 when it should be Level 2. All were corrected in the accounts. This suggests weaknesses in the Fund's processes for initially classifying investments by fair value hierarchy.
findings.matters: Correct fair value classification is essential for audit and regulatory compliance. The scale of misclassifications (£308m combined) indicates control weaknesses in investment categorization that could mask valuation issues and affect financial reporting reliability.
findings.figures: £13.6m, £285.3m, and £9.2m misclassifications totalling £308.1m across three investments
findings.quote: One Pooled property investment and one pooled investment was mistakenly classified as Level 1 investment which were then re-classified to Level 2 amounting to £13.6m and £285.3m respectively. One pooled property investment was mistakenly classified as Level 3 investment which was then re-classified to Level 2 amounting to £9.2m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Grant Thornton's Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Investment valuation adjustments of £10.6m identified during audit due to timing lags in receiving capital statements
findings.detail: The Fund's draft accounts undervalued Level 3 investments by £10.187m and overvalued Level 2 investments by £393k due to timing differences between when valuations were available for account preparation versus when final capital statements were received. Management identified and corrected these through post-year-end journal entries. Auditor concluded this timing lag 'is not uncommon in the sector' and does not constitute a control weakness.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the fund's investment valuations are reliable and whether controls over valuation timing are adequate. Material timing adjustments post-close suggest processes for obtaining timely investment data need strengthening.
findings.figures: £10.187m L3 assets adjustment, £393k L2 assets adjustment, net increase to Net Assets of £9.794m to £3,748.2m
findings.quote: there was a timing lag between the investment valuation information for certain Level 3 assets being available to the Fund when it had to prepare its accounts and final capital statements being received which resulted in under-valuation of Level 3 assets by £10.187m

findings.paper_title: West Northants Council External Audit Results Report 2024-25 - Appendix A
findings.headline: Six financial statement adjustments made during audit resulting in £21.741m change to Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement with no impact on general fund
findings.detail: The auditors identified and adjusted six items during the audit, resulting in a net £21.741m adjustment to the CIES. While this has no impact on the general fund, it indicates material errors in the draft accounts that management did not identify.
findings.matters: Multiple material adjustments signal control weaknesses in the accounts production process. Even if general fund-neutral, they indicate the council's management team did not detect significant errors before audit.
findings.figures: Six adjustments, £21.741m total change to CIES
findings.quote: We have identified six adjustments to the financial statements, resulting in a £21.741m adjustment to the Council's Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement, there is no impact on the general fund.

findings.paper_title: West Northants Council External Audit Results Report 2024-25 - Appendix A
findings.headline: Material IFRS 16 implementation added £258m right-of-use assets and £254m lease liabilities to balance sheet
findings.detail: The new leasing standard (IFRS 16, effective from 1 April 2024) required recognition of £258m of right-of-use assets and £254m of lease liabilities, including peppercorn rental arrangements. This was assessed as a significant risk due to complexity, though the auditors have completed their work on this.
findings.matters: The £254m increase in liabilities materially affects debt ratios and gearing calculations used by lenders to assess borrowing capacity. The new obligation structure affects cash flow forecasting and debt service coverage.
findings.figures: £258m right-of-use assets, £254m lease liabilities
findings.quote: The implementation of IFRS 16 has had a material impact on the Authority's financial statement with £258m of right of use assets and a £254m lease liability being recognised in the draft financial statements.

findings.paper_title: West Northants Council External Audit Results Report 2024-25 - Appendix A
findings.headline: Pension liability accounting error: £173.92m pension asset ceiling adjustment posted to wrong line of accounts
findings.detail: An adjustment relating to the pension asset ceiling (£173.92m) was incorrectly posted to employee benefit expenditure within Net Cost of Services when it should have been posted to Remeasurement of the net defined benefit liability within the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement. This misclassification affects the presentation of pension costs.
findings.matters: A £173.92m mispostings indicates control weaknesses in pension accounting. Incorrect presentation obscures the true cost of pension obligations and the council's service delivery costs.
findings.figures: £173.92m pension asset ceiling adjustment
findings.quote: the adjustment relating to the pension asset ceiling (£173.92m) had been incorrectly posted to employee benefit expenditure within the Net Cost of Services when it should have been posted to the Remeasurement of the net defined benefit liability / (asset) line within the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement.

findings.paper_title: West Northants Council External Audit Results Report 2024-25 - Appendix A
findings.headline: HRA dwelling valuations understated by estimated £2.131m; garages had incorrect unit pricing
findings.detail: Testing of HRA garages identified understatement of £0.998m due to valuer using incorrect garage unit price and including an erroneous land valuation. This error has been extrapolated across total Housing Land & Buildings revalued in the year (£16.539m) to give potential net understatement of £2.131m.
findings.matters: Housing stock valuations affect HRA borrowing capacity and subsidy calculations. Consistent valuation errors suggest inadequate expert oversight and create uncertainty about housing asset value to lenders.
findings.figures: Garages understatement £0.998m, Housing Land & Buildings total £16.539m, extrapolated understatement £2.131m
findings.quote: Our testing identified that the valuations for HRA Garages were understated by amount of £0.998m due to the valuer using the incorrect garage unit price and including a land valuation in their original valuation. We have extrapolated this error across the total Housing Land & Buildings revalued during the year (£16.539m) to give a potential understatement of £2.131m.

findings.headline: Significant VFM weaknesses identified in Dedicated Schools Grant deficit and housing stock oversight
findings.detail: The auditors have identified significant weaknesses in the council's Value for Money arrangements specifically around the DSG deficit and oversight of housing stock and finances. These are reported separately in the Auditor's Annual Report accompanying this findings document.
findings.matters: DSG deficits signal inability to manage school funding pressures and can trigger government intervention. Housing finance weaknesses indicate poor property asset stewardship affecting HRA sustainability and borrowing capacity.
